# Recap: Pt. 1 in five minutes {background-color="#006633" .section-slide}

5 minutes

## Start-up

Open your project by double-clicking the `.Rproj` file, then run:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(here)
library(broom)     # new today: tidy model results
library(emmeans)   # new today: group comparisons
```

::: {.live}
→ Check: does `getwd()` show your project folder?
:::

::: notes
Anyone who missed Pt. 1 or lost their project: create a new project now (File → New Project) and install packages from the Pt. 1 code file while we recap.
:::

## Quick check [3 min]{.timer}

::: {.exercise}
1. What does `x <- 5` do?
2. In `mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)`, what is the function and what are the arguments?
3. If `temps <- c(18, 25, 31)`, what does `temps[temps > 24]` give?
:::

. . .

1. Stores the value 5 under the name `x`
2. Function `mean`; arguments `x` and `na.rm = TRUE`
3. `25 31`: the values where the condition is `TRUE`

## A data frame is a table of vectors

Each **column** is a vector, like the ones you made in Pt. 1. Each **row** is one observation.

```{r}
#| output-location: column
penguins$body_mass_g[1:6]

mean(penguins$body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
```

<br>

`$` pulls one column out of a table: `table$column`. Today you'll mostly refer to columns **by name** inside functions instead.

# Part 1: Wrangling data {background-color="#006633" .section-slide}

30 minutes

## The pipe `|>`: "and then"

Most analyses are a chain of steps. There are two ways to write a chain:

| | Nested: read inside out | Piped: read left to right |
|---|---|---|
| **Math** | g(f(x)) | x → f → g |
| **Everyday** | bake(mix(sift(flour))) | take flour, **and then** sift, **and then** mix, **and then** bake |
| **R** | `round(mean(c(1.2, 5.7)), 1)` | `c(1.2, 5.7) |> mean() |> round(1)` |

: {tbl-colwidths="[14,43,43]"}

<br>

`|>` passes the result on the left into the first argument of the function on the right. Shortcut: **Ctrl+Shift+M** / **Cmd+Shift+M**.

::: notes
If the shortcut types %>% instead: Tools → Global Options → Code → tick "Use native pipe operator". %>% works the same way for today's purposes.
:::

## Five verbs do most of the work

| Verb | What it does | Spreadsheet equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| `filter()` | Keep rows that meet a condition | Filter menu |
| `select()` | Keep or drop columns | Hide columns |
| `arrange()` | Sort rows | Sort button |
| `mutate()` | Add or change a column | New column with a formula, filled down |
| `summarise()` | Collapse rows into a summary | Pivot table |

<br>

Each one takes a data frame in and gives a data frame back, so they chain together with `|>`.

## `filter()`: keep rows

Uses the **conditions** from Pt. 1. A comma means "and".

```{r}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Gentoo", body_mass_g > 5800)
```

## `select()` and `arrange()`: choose columns, sort rows

```{r}
penguins |>
  select(species, island, body_mass_g) |>
  arrange(desc(body_mass_g))       # desc() = largest first
```

::: {.small .muted}
R shows the first few rows and tells you how many more there are.
:::

## `mutate()`: add a column

Like typing a formula in a new spreadsheet column and filling it down.

```{r}
penguins |>
  mutate(mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000) |>
  select(species, body_mass_g, mass_kg)
```

## `group_by()` + `summarise()`: the pivot table

```{=html}
<div class="flow">
  <div class="box">344 penguins<span class="lbl">one table</span></div>
  <div class="arrow">→</div>
  <div class="box fn">group_by(species)<span class="lbl">split</span></div>
  <div class="arrow">→</div>
  <div class="box fn">summarise(…)<span class="lbl">summarise each group</span></div>
  <div class="arrow">→</div>
  <div class="box">3 rows<span class="lbl">one per species</span></div>
</div>
```

```{r}
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_g = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_g = sd(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE))
```

## Exercise: wrangle [5 min]{.timer}

::: {.exercise}
1. Keep only penguins from **Dream** island.
2. Add a column `bill_ratio` = bill length ÷ bill depth.
3. Find the mean `bill_ratio` per species, highest first.
:::

. . .

```{r}
#| output-location: column
penguins |>
  filter(island == "Dream") |>
  mutate(bill_ratio =
    bill_length_mm / bill_depth_mm) |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(mean_ratio =
    mean(bill_ratio, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_ratio))
```

## Reshape: wide to long

Remember tidy data from Pt. 1? `pivot_longer()` fixes data with a variable hidden in the column names.

```{r}
#| include: false
scores <- tibble(id = 1:2, week1 = c(5.1, 4.8), week2 = c(5.6, 5.0))
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
scores
```
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
scores |>
  pivot_longer(c(week1, week2),
               names_to = "week",
               values_to = "score")
```
:::
::::

::: {.small .muted}
`pivot_wider()` goes the other way.
:::

## Cleaning messy column names

Real exports have names like `"Body Mass (g)"`, which are awkward to type. `clean_names()` from the **janitor** package fixes them all at once.

```{r}
names(penguins_raw)[10:13]
```

```{r}
clean <- janitor::clean_names(penguins_raw)
names(clean)[10:13]
```

::: {.small .muted}
`janitor::clean_names()` means "the `clean_names` function from the janitor package", without loading the whole package with `library()`.
:::

# Part 2: Figures with ggplot2 {background-color="#006633" .section-slide}

30 minutes

## A plot is three choices

Describe a chart to a colleague and you've already written it:

> "Using the **penguins** data, put **flipper length** on the x-axis and **body mass** on the y-axis, colour by **species**, and draw **points**."

| Choice | In the sentence | In ggplot2 |
|---|---|---|
| **Data** | the penguins data | `ggplot(penguins, …)` |
| **Aesthetics**: which column goes where | flipper length on x, mass on y, colour by species | `aes(x = …, y = …, colour = …)` |
| **Geometry**: what shape to draw | points | `geom_point()` |

: {tbl-colwidths="[30,40,30]"}

## Build it up: 1. data and axes

```{r}
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5
ggplot(penguins,
       aes(x = flipper_length_mm,
           y = body_mass_g))
```

<br>

Axes, but nothing drawn yet: we haven't chosen a geometry.

## Build it up: 2. add points

```{r}
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5
ggplot(penguins,
       aes(x = flipper_length_mm,
           y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point()
```

<br>

Layers are added with **`+`**, not `|>`. Mixing them up is a common slip.

## Build it up: 3. colour and labels

```{r}
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5
ggplot(penguins,
       aes(x = flipper_length_mm,
           y = body_mass_g,
           colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)",
       y = "Body mass (g)",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

## Which plot for which question?

| Question | Geometry |
|---|---|
| How do two measurements relate? | `geom_point()`, plus `geom_smooth(method = "lm")` for a trend line |
| How is one measurement spread across groups? | `geom_boxplot()` with `geom_jitter()` on top |
| How does something change over time? | `geom_line()` |
| How many in each category? | `geom_bar()` |
| What does one measurement's distribution look like? | `geom_histogram()` |

## Show the data, not just the average

A bar of means hides how many points there are and how they're spread. Show them.

```{r}
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5
ggplot(penguins,
       aes(x = species,
           y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15,
              alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(x = NULL,
       y = "Body mass (g)")
```

## Small multiples: one panel per group

```{r}
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
ggplot(penguins,
       aes(x = flipper_length_mm,
           y = body_mass_g,
           colour = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ island) +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

`facet_wrap(~ island)`: "one panel for each island". Often clearer than many colours on one panel.

## Save figures from code

```{r}
#| eval: false
my_plot <- ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point()

ggsave(here("figures", "fig1.pdf"), my_plot,
       width = 85, height = 70, units = "mm")       # vector: sharp at any size

ggsave(here("figures", "fig1.png"), my_plot,
       width = 85, height = 70, units = "mm", dpi = 600)
```

<br>

- Saving from code records the size and resolution, so the figure is identical every time.
- Journals often want single-column figures 85–90 mm wide and double-column 170–180 mm. Check your journal's guide.

## Exercise: plot [5 min]{.timer}

::: {.exercise}
1. Make a boxplot of **bill depth** by species, with the points on top.
2. Then give each **sex** its own panel. First drop missing sex with `filter()`. Hint: `!` means NOT, so `!is.na(sex)` is TRUE when sex is **not** missing.
:::

. . .

```{r}
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species,
             y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ sex) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Bill depth (mm)")
```

# Part 3: Statistics {background-color="#006633" .section-slide}

35 minutes

## Formulas: "explained by"

R's statistics functions describe a model with `~`, read as **"explained by"**.

| | Example |
|---|---|
| **Math** | y = f(x): y depends on x |
| **Everyday** | "Does body mass depend on species?" |
| **R** | `body_mass_g ~ species` |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20,80]"}

<br>

| Formula | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `y ~ x` | y explained by x |
| `y ~ x1 + x2` | y explained by x1 and x2 together |
| `y ~ x1 * x2` | the same, plus: does the effect of x1 depend on x2? (interaction) |

## Which test?

| Question | Test | R function |
|---|---|---|
| Do **two** groups differ on average? | t-test | `t.test(y ~ group)` |
| Do **three or more** groups differ? | ANOVA | `aov(y ~ group)` |
| How does y change with x, accounting for other variables? | Linear regression | `lm(y ~ x1 + x2)` |

<br>

All three take a formula and `data =`, so once you can write one, you can write them all.

## t-test: do male and female Adelie differ in mass?

```{r}
adelie <- penguins |> filter(species == "Adelie", !is.na(sex))

t.test(body_mass_g ~ sex, data = adelie)
```

::: notes
R uses Welch's t-test by default, which doesn't assume equal variances. That's the safer choice. wilcox.test() is the non-parametric alternative.
:::

## ANOVA: three or more groups

Does body mass differ between the three species?

```{r}
fit_aov <- aov(body_mass_g ~ species, data = penguins)
summary(fit_aov)
```

<br>

A small p-value (`Pr(>F)`) says **at least one** species differs. It doesn't say which.

## Which groups differ?

A **post-hoc** test compares every pair, adjusting for doing several tests at once.

```{r}
emmeans(fit_aov, pairwise ~ species)$contrasts
```

<br>

Gentoo differ from both other species; Adelie and Chinstrap don't differ clearly.

## Linear regression

How does body mass change with flipper length, accounting for species?

```{r}
fit_lm <- lm(body_mass_g ~ flipper_length_mm + species, data = penguins)
```

`tidy()` from the **broom** package turns the result into a table:

```{r}
tidy(fit_lm, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)
```

## Reading the coefficients

```{r}
#| include: false
co <- tidy(fit_lm, conf.int = TRUE)
fl <- co[co$term == "flipper_length_mm", ]
gen <- co[co$term == "speciesGentoo", ]
```

| Term | Means |
|---|---|
| `flipper_length_mm` | Each extra mm of flipper adds about **`r round(fl$estimate, 1)` g**, within a species |
| `speciesChinstrap`, `speciesGentoo` | Difference from **Adelie** at the same flipper length. Gentoo: **`r round(gen$estimate)` g** heavier |
| `(Intercept)` | Predicted mass for an Adelie with 0 mm flippers. A math anchor, not a real penguin |

: {tbl-colwidths="[32,68]"}

<br>

Why compared with Adelie? It's the **first factor level**, which becomes the reference group (Pt. 1, factors).

## Check the assumptions

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3.5
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(fit_lm, which = 1:2)
```

::: {.small}
**Left:** no curve or funnel shape → the relationship is straight and the spread is even. **Right:** points near the line → residuals are roughly normal.
:::

## Report it

Give the estimate, its confidence interval, the test statistic and p-value, and the sample size.

> Body mass increased by `r round(fl$estimate, 1)` g per mm of flipper length (95% CI `r round(fl$conf.low, 1)` to `r round(fl$conf.high, 1)`; t(`r fit_lm$df.residual`) = `r round(fl$statistic, 1)`, p < 0.001), controlling for species (n = `r nobs(fit_lm)`).

<br>

Every number in that sentence came from R, not typed by hand. Part 4 shows how to keep it that way.

## Exercise: statistics [5 min]{.timer}

::: {.exercise}
Do male and female **Gentoo** penguins differ in **flipper length**?

1. Make a data frame of Gentoo penguins with a recorded sex.
2. Run a t-test.
3. Write one sentence reporting the result.
:::

. . .

```{r}
#| include: false
gentoo_tt <- t.test(flipper_length_mm ~ sex,
                    data = filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo", !is.na(sex)))
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| eval: false
gentoo <- penguins |>
  filter(species == "Gentoo", !is.na(sex))

t.test(flipper_length_mm ~ sex, data = gentoo)
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
Males' flippers were longer by about **`r round(abs(diff(gentoo_tt$estimate)), 1)` mm** (95% CI `r round(abs(gentoo_tt$conf.int[2]), 1)` to `r round(abs(gentoo_tt$conf.int[1]), 1)` mm; p < 0.001).
:::
::::

## Beyond today

| Your data | Model | Package |
|---|---|---|
| Repeated measures, people within groups | Mixed model | lme4 |
| Yes/no outcomes, counts, proportions | Generalized linear model | base R: `glm()` |
| Curved trends | Generalized additive model | mgcv |
| Time until an event | Survival analysis | survival |

<br>

Same formula idea throughout: `outcome ~ predictors`.

# Part 4: Reproducible reports {background-color="#006633" .section-slide}

15 minutes

## The copy-paste problem

::: {.incremental}
- You run the analysis, then **type** the numbers into Word and paste in the figures.
- A reviewer asks you to drop three outliers.
- Now every number, table and figure has to be found and fixed by hand. Something gets missed.
:::

. . .

**Quarto** puts the text, the code and its results in one file. Change the data, click **Render**, and everything updates.

## A Quarto document has three parts

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
**1. Header**: settings

```yaml
---
title: "Penguin report"
author: "Your Name"
format: html
---
```
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
**2. Text**: written normally

```markdown
## Results

Gentoo penguins were
the heaviest species.
```
:::
::: {.column width="34%"}
**3. Code chunks**: run R

```{{r}}
fit <- lm(body_mass_g ~
  species, data = penguins)
```
:::
::::

<br>

File → New File → **Quarto Document**. Click **Render** (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+K) to produce HTML, Word or PDF.

## Inline code: numbers that write themselves

Put R code inside a sentence with a backtick and `r`:

```markdown
The study measured `r knitr::inline_expr("nrow(penguins)")` penguins
of `r knitr::inline_expr("n_distinct(penguins$species)")` species.
```

When you render, that becomes:

> The study measured `r nrow(penguins)` penguins of `r n_distinct(penguins$species)` species.

<br>

Change the data and re-render, and the sentence updates itself.

## Try it [5 min]{.timer}

::: {.exercise}
1. File → New File → Quarto Document. Give it a title, untick "Use visual markdown editor", click Create.
2. Delete the example text. Add a chunk (**Ctrl+Alt+I** / **Cmd+Option+I**) with `library(tidyverse)`, `library(palmerpenguins)` and one plot from today.
3. Write one sentence with an inline number, such as the number of penguins: `` `r knitr::inline_expr("nrow(penguins)")` ``.
4. Save it in your project and click **Render**.
:::

## Make it last

| Tool | What it does | Command |
|---|---|---|
| **Quarto** | Report regenerates from code | Render |
| **renv** | Records the exact package versions you used | `renv::init()`, then `renv::snapshot()` |
| `sessionInfo()` | Prints R and package versions; put it at the end of reports | `sessionInfo()` |
| **Git + GitHub** | A history of every change, and a backup | RStudio's Git pane |

<br>

**The test:** restart R, render the report. If it works, your analysis is reproducible.

# Wrap-up {background-color="#006633" .section-slide}

## Take-home project

::: {.exercise}
In your RStudio Project, write one Quarto report that:

1. Reads `data/raw/penguins_raw.csv` and cleans the column names
2. Makes one summary table with `group_by()` and `summarise()`
3. Makes one figure and saves it with `ggsave()`
4. Runs one statistical test and reports it with inline numbers
5. Ends with `sessionInfo()`

Restart R and render. If it renders, you're done.
:::
